results.notes: CRITICAL PRODUCT-IDENTITY ISSUE: both documents that name OUHR-1 place it under a MARS section, not a lunar one. In simulants.html (ESRIC knowledge base, saved from http://knowledge.esric.lu/simulants/) the row for 'OUHR-1 and HR-2' sits under the <h2> heading 'Mars Regolith Simulants' (a separate heading 'Lunar Regolith Simulants' exists earlier in the same page and does not contain this product). In the ISECG 2021 ISRU Technology Gap Assessment Report, Table 9 (p.62) lists 'OUHR-1 and HR-2' in the ESA/Open University block explicitly under a 'Mars' subsection heading, sandwiched between other clearly-Martian ESA engineering soils (ES-1..ES-4) and other Open University Mars products (OUCM-1/CM-2 'Contemporary Martian Simulants', OUEB-1/EB-2 'Early basaltic', OUSR-1/SR-2 'Sulfur rich') — all Mars analogues, none lunar. No document in the library states OUHR-1 is a lunar regolith simulant. This strongly suggests OUHR-1 (and its pair HR-2, S146) does not belong in the Lunar Regolith Simulant Database at all, or was miscategorized from a mixed lunar+Mars source list. A curator should decide whether to remove/relabel this entry. Additionally: both sources always list 'OUHR-1 and HR-2' as one combined table row/entry (like ES-4='Mixture of ES-1 and ES-3', OUCM-1/CM-2, OUEB-1/EB-2, OUSR-1/SR-2 are also paired in the same tables) — no document anywhere gives OUHR-1 and HR-2 separate/distinguishing data, so it is unclear if they are two grades of one simulant or two distinct products; treat any single number found for the pair as applying loosely to both, not confirmed individually. Full library sweep (grep -rliw over Sources_text, both hyphenated 'OUHR-1'/'HR-2' and unhyphenated 'OUHR1'/'HR2') found no other documents naming this product beyond the two already listed.

Mars Regolith Simulants

, which is separate from the earlier 'Lunar Regolith Simulants' h2.

checks.notes:
The Mars classification is confirmed. In ISECG Table 9 (PDF p.63) an orange 'Mars' sub-header row inside the ESA block sits above ES-1..ES-4, OUCM-1 and CM-2, OUEB-1 and EB-2, OUHR-1 and HR-2, and OUSR-1 and SR-2. ESRIC lists the entry under 'Mars Regolith Simulants'. None of the sources calls it a lunar simulant.

The extractor missed one document. papers/LRS/Sources/Abrasion Evaluation of Moon and Mars Simulants.html is a NotebookLM capture of Barko, Kalacska, Keresztes, Zsidai, Shegawu, Kalacska, 'Abrasion Evaluation of Moon and Mars Simulants on Rotating Shaft/Sealing Materials: Simulants and Structural Materials Review and Selection', Preprints.org, DOI 10.20944/preprints202306.1135.v1 (2023). Its Table 21, 'Comparison of Martian simulants', has the row 'OUCM一OUEB一OUHR一OUSR | Open University | UK | Astrobiology simulants. Each has a standard composition (-1) and adjusted Fe 2+ concentration (-2). | 200 – 2000 µm'. The extractor's grep -w 'OUHR-1' did not find it because the text uses '一' separators and the file is not in Sources_text. It is a review that names only the family 'OUHR', not 'OUHR-1', so I did not add it as a reference. It does settle the extractor's open question: -1 is the standard composition and -2 is a variant with adjusted Fe2+. So OUHR-1 and HR-2 are two distinct products, and the combined-row values in ISECG and ESRIC apply to the pair, not to either one individually. It also puts the product under Martian simulants.

R167 and R168 both point to the same ISECG report.

Other Sources-tree hits are the project's own Global Registry and dashboard captures (not evidence) and the NotebookLM capture of the ISECG report (the same document). The Sources_text sweeps found only the two listed documents: 'OUHR-1' in 2 files, 'OUHR1' in 0, 'OUHR' in 2.

problems: 'HR-2' appears only inside the combined row 'OUHR-1 and HR-2', and the row is verbatim.
The table is on PDF page 63 (unnumbered, after the printed 'Page 62' footer), not p.62.

The name follows the table's pattern ('OUCM-1 and CM-2', 'OUEB-1 and EB-2', 'OUSR-1 and SR-2'), in which the shared 'OU' prefix is dropped from the second name. So 'HR-2' is most likely short for OUHR-2, and the database name 'HR-2' looks like a split of that shorthand. This is an inference; no document spells out 'OUHR-2'.
Same situation as S145: 'HR-2' occurs once in the raw HTML, in 'Name OUHR-1 and HR-2', under the 'Mars Regolith Simulants' h2 (div id=marsregolith).
The quote is a concatenation of separate fields, each verbatim.
Stored 'Unavailable' is contradicted: ESRIC says 'Availability Currently available' for 'OUHR-1 and HR-2'.
ISECG Table 9 (PDF p.63) says the same explicitly, not implicitly: the row's Supply Confidence cell is green, and the Key on that page defines green as '= Currently available'.
The value comes from the combined row, not from an HR-2-specific statement.
'Haematite rich' is verbatim in the ISECG Type column (PDF p.63) and the ESRIC Description. It describes the combined pair and is not a lunar sample reference, so the field does not fit.
'Open University' is verbatim in the ISECG Info and Contact columns (PDF p.63, ESA block) and in the ESRIC Supplier/Contact field.

checks.notes:
The extractor's step from 'possible' to 'names_simulant=true' is correct: each document has exactly one 'HR-2', and it is inside the combined OUHR-1 entry.

The extractor also missed the NotebookLM capture papers/LRS/Sources/Abrasion Evaluation of Moon and Mars Simulants.html (original: Barko et al., Preprints.org, DOI 10.20944/preprints202306.1135.v1). Its Table 21 ('Comparison of Martian simulants') says of the OU family 'OUCM一OUEB一OUHR一OUSR': 'Each has a standard composition (-1) and adjusted Fe 2+ concentration (-2).' That identifies HR-2 (OUHR-2) as the adjusted-Fe2+ variant, a different product from OUHR-1. The curator should consider renaming S146 to OUHR-2 and noting that its stored values come only from the combined pair row. The same table gives a particle size range of '200 – 2000 µm' for the whole family, which is not a stored field or a product-specific value.

The Mars classification is confirmed in both sources, so the entry probably does not belong in a lunar database.

The library sweep over Sources_text found 'HR-2' in 2 files (the listed ones) and 'HR2' in 0. The Sources tree also holds the project's own Global Registry and dashboard captures, which are not evidence.

Opened files/1643/S2095268624001381.html (doi 10.1016/j.ijmst.2024.09.005). The inventory table reads 'Korea 2 KLS-1 [58] , KOHLS-1 [59] /KAUMLS [60]', and [60] is Yoo et al. 2014. The usage sentence is verbatim apart from spacing: "Lee et al. [155] , [156] , [157] mixed thermoplastic polyethylene ( w =10%, d <75 μm) and KAUMLS simulants ( w =90%, d <75 μm) to develop LRSPC, with a compressive strength of 13 MPa." It is a review and usage document, not a primary source.

The NEW1 header is verbatim: 'J. of The Korean Society for Aeronautical and Space Sciences 42(12), 1037-1044(2014)'. It is the journal year of the paper that developed KAUMLS. Corroboration: Kang 2024 Table 1 has 'KAUMLS | 한국 | 2014년 | -', and R081 (Ryu 2018) says attempts were made "in 2010 (Hanyang University) and 2014 (Korea Aerospace University) (Kim et al. 2014; Yoo et al. 2014)".
Agree: none of R173, NEW1, NEW2 or Kang 2024 states an availability status for KAUMLS.

Agree that 'General' is unsupported, but the extractor's reasoning is wrong, and the stored value is contradicted, not merely unsourced. NEW1 does tie KAUMLS to a specific Apollo sample. p.1039, §2.2: "복제토 개발에서 기준으로 사용한 달 토양의 샘플인 lunar soil 14163의 입도 분포는 Fig. 3과 같으며, bearing capacity는 4.45 kPa/cm이다." (the reference lunar-soil sample for the simulant's development is lunar soil 14163). p.1040: "KAUMLS는 6개의 표준체에 의해 개발되었기 때문에 lunar soil 14163의 평균입도와 다소 차이를 보이나 전반적인 입도 분포는 달 토양을 모사함을 확인 하였다." Fig. 5 plots 'Lunar Soil 14163' against 'KAUMLS'. Lunar soil 14163 is an Apollo 14 sample (Table 1 column 'Lunar Soil 14163' beside 'Apollo 14'). The supported value is Apollo 14 (lunar soil 14163, for grain-size distribution and bearing capacity), not 'General'.

NEW1 p.1037 affiliation, verbatim: 'Department of Aerospace and Mechanical Engineering, Graduate School at Korea Aerospace University'. Author 4 is at 'Department of Aerospace and Mechanical Engineering, Korea Aerospace University'.

checks.notes: (1) Verified: NEW1 p.1039 says chemical composition was deliberately not simulated: '충격흡수 성능에 관여하지 않는 화학적 성분은 고려하지 않고 입자크기(grain size)와, 입도분포, 입자밀도 등 기계적 성질만 만족하는 달 복제토를 개발하였다'. No composition appears in the defining paper, so this is a candidate for 'not_published' rather than 'not_extracted'. Table 1 on that page shows compositions only for Apollo 14, 14163, CAS-1, JSC-1, FJS-1 and KOHLS-1, not KAUMLS. (2) NEW1 Table 2 grain-size recipe verified (weight %): 2360-1180 um 4; 1180-600 6; 600-300 8; 300-150 10; 150-75 17; finer than 75 55. This is a design recipe from six sieves, not a measured D50. (3) NEW1 Table 3, p.1040, has plate-indentation bearing capacity that the extractor did not mention: at indentation area 425.5 cm2, KAUMLS depth 1.17 cm and bearing capacity 5.59 kPa/cm; at 136.0 cm2, 0.94 cm and 7.47 kPa/cm (dry sand: 33.53 and 41.79). This field is probably not tracked in the database. (4) Kang 2024 (S031 NEW2) describes KAUMLS as made from dry ordinary sand ('건조한 일반 모래를 원료로 KAUMLS을 개발하였고[30]'). Its abstract groups KAUMLS with mare-like simulants, while its Table 1 soil-type cell for KAUMLS is '-'. Those statements are inconsistent, so neither is a reliable source for the mare/highland type. (5) Library sweep: grep -rliw 'KAUMLS' finds only files/1643 and files/1793. 'KAU-MLS' finds nothing. 'Korea Aerospace University' also hits the Ryu 2018 PDF (Yoo et al. 2014 cited without the product name) and the IGG-01 page (files/1757), which cites Yoo 2014 as [20] but uses it for KOHLS-1, not KAUMLS. results.notes: MAJOR FINDING: I could not find any document that independently characterizes a real, distinct product literally named 'CUG-1' (i.e., without a suffix letter). Every occurrence of the bare string 'CUG-1' that I could trace via its own citation resolves to X.X. He, L. Xiao et al. (2010), 'Lunar Regolith Simulant CUG-1A', 41st LPSC abstract #1183 — the exact same paper already serving as reference R076 for sibling simulant S012 (CUG-1A) — with the trailing 'A' dropped in secondary citing text: (1) the LEAG-SIM-SAT-2010 Appendix-4 table (NEW1) lists 'CUG-1 | He et al, 2010'; (2) Taylor, Pieters & Britt 2016 Table 2 (NEW2) lists 'CUG-1' with an apparently erroneous developer attribution ('Chinese Academy of Sciences' — contradicted by every other source, which gives China University of Geosciences); (3) Li et al. 2022 (the CUMT-1 paper, listed for S125 as both papers/LRS/1-s2.0-S2095268621001002-main.pdf and its duplicate at .../1713/) cites '... CUG-1 [35] ...' in its intro, and its own reference [35] reads 'Lunar regolith simulant CUG-1A' — confirming the abbreviation; (4) the ResearchGate 'citations' preview snippets embedded on the TJ-1 page (doc 1765) and the NEU-1 page (doc 1712) show the same '[35]'-sourced 'CUG-1' text, while those pages' own abstracts correctly say 'CUG-1A'. I therefore judged names_simulant=false for all of these when they appeared only as citation-preview noise, and did not add them as new_references (only the three primary-looking documents NEW1–NEW3 were added, per the 4-document sweep cap). A fifth candidate, doc 1641 ('How to make lunar soil suitable for cultivation?'), instead attributes 'CUG-1' to 'Z. Yao et al., 2022b' — but that citation most likely refers to a genuinely different, later variant, 'CUG-1B' (Yao, Feng & Liu 2022, Acta Astronautica 193), which I could not access to confirm (see unavailable_documents). R151 (Patzwald et al. 2025), the only formally-listed reference for S125, in fact discusses 'CUG-1A' (with a stray OCR space, 'CUG-1 A'), not 'CUG-1' — so it does not name this exact product string and is marked names_simulant=false. Net assessment: S125 has no independent evidentiary basis distinct from S012/CUG-1A. Strongly recommend the curator verify whether S125 is a duplicate database entry that should be merged into or removed in favor of S012, or whether it should instead be re-pointed at the distinct 'CUG-1B' product (Yao et al. 2022) — for which no data are currently in this group's document set.

results.notes: Engelschion et al. 2020 (R124) also reports an absolute/particle density of 3.08 g/cm3 for NU-LHT-3M ('The absolute density measurements ... of EAC-1, JSC-1A, JSC-2A, DNA and NU-LHT-3M resulted in 2.90, 2.92, 2.89, 2.79 and 3.08 g/cm3 respectively', p.3) — no matching scalar field exists in this schema (only bulk_density), flagging for curator in case a particle/absolute-density field should be added. Same paper (p.3) states 'There are no published data on the cohesion of DNA or NU-LHT-3M, but it is considered to be negligible in NU-LHT-2M' — so cohesion should NOT be filled in from any inferred/negligible value. It also reports NU-LHT-3M is 'fully crystallised' (DSC shows a melting endotherm but no glass transition), i.e. essentially 0% glass, but gives no quantified percentage, so this is not entered as a mineral value. Two supply-chain descriptions conflict: Engelschion et al. 2020 (R124) attributes NU-LHT-3M's production to 'Zybek Advanced Products Inc.', while the Slabic Guide (NEW3) and 2022 Assessment (NEW2) attribute it to NASA Glenn Research Center / USGS (Steve Wilson) using Stillwater anorthosite+norite+mill sand — curator should reconcile which supplier record is authoritative. The ISECG 2021 ISRU Technology Gap Assessment Report (papers/agent-fetched/ISECG_2021_ISRU_Technology_Gap_Assessment_Report_Apr2021.pdf, p.~46) mentions NU-LHT-3M only as one of several simulants used at a TU Munich test facility — a usage mention with no characterization data, not opened for values per the sweep rules.

results.notes: MAJOR FLAG: the database names this product 'NU-LHT-5M', but per Rickman et al. 2024 (p.6): 'Originally to be named NU-LHT-5M, the name has subsequently been changed to NUW-LHT-5M in recognition of the fabricator, including the glass: Washington Mills, Niagara Falls, NY.' Every substantive document in the library (the 2024 characterization report, the 2024 Lunar Simulant Assessment Report, the Slabic Guide) refers to this simulant as 'NUW-LHT-5M', never as plain 'NU-LHT-5M' — the plain name is only used historically/in passing as the pre-rename working title. I have treated all NUW-LHT-5M data above as pertaining to this same DB entry given the explicit rename statement, but recommend the curator rename the product to 'NUW-LHT-5M' for consistency with the literature. R125's citation ('Lunar Simulants Assessment', no year/doi/url given) is ambiguous between the '2022 Lunar Simulants Assessment Final.pdf' and '2024_Lunar_Simulant_Assessment_Report.pdf' (both carry that generic title, and both are listed under S090's library_documents_naming_it). Only the 2024 report substantively discusses this product (spectroscopy comparison, quoted above); the 2022 report mentions 'NU-LHT-5M' solely inside its own bibliography (a 2022 LPSC abstract title, 'Design of NU-LHT-5M and -6M'), not in its body text, so it does not itself characterize the product — I resolved R125 against the 2024 report. The Table 4.1 mineral wt% values (Bytownite, Pyroxenes, Olivine, etc.) are normalized to the crystalline/glass-free fraction only, which the table caption states is 60% of the whole simulant (NUW-LHT-5M being ~40% glass overall) — these are NOT wt% of the bulk product; curator should decide how to store fraction-normalized values or whether to convert them. Table 4.4 also gives two earlier UTSA test batches (Test 1, Test 2) with lower Fe2O3 (~3.2 vs 4.31 in the current-production WM row) — the text explains 'Test 1 and Test 2 had less Fe than the design specified. Changes to production methods enabled Washington Mills to raise the Fe closer to the target' (p.12), i.e. an evolving product; I reported only the current-production (WM) row as new_values. Table 10.2 also lists a JSC-lab bulk density range of 1.27-1.30 for NUW-LHT-5M and an Alfred as-received value of 1.25, both omitted from new_values (range/duplicate) but available in the source table if the curator wants them.

The metadata is wrong. 'Metz France Keynote' is only the file name. The deck's actual title is 'Lunar Regolith Simulants: Current Simulants, Use Cases, Selection Process, and Best Practices', by Dr. Heather Oravec, The University of Akron at NASA Glenn Research Center. The authors field should not be blank.
Verbatim at printed p.20: 'Small amounts of the -2E and -2EG simulants still exist for NASA testing purposes.' This supports 'Limited Stock' directly.

The quote is verbatim, but it is on printed p.18, and the full sentence speaks of the whole series: 'The two dominant rocks in the NU-LHT simulants were Anorthosite and Norite ... with the primary purpose of creating a noritic anorthosite simulant like the Apollo 16 regolith samples'. No document ties NU-LHT-2EG specifically to Apollo 16. -2EG was an engineering-grade material made from mill sand plus agglutinate. Metz slide 17 and Patzwald 2025 p.203 are also series-level only.

The extractor's quote is verbatim at p.18 but describes the series. A product-specific anchor is available at printed p.19: 'NASA and USGS experimented with other prototypes, referring to them as the following (Gruener, 2023).' That sentence introduces the list that includes NU-LHT-2EG. Rickman et al. 2024 (Acknowledgments, printed p.36-37) adds that Stephen Wilson of the USGS did 'grinding, milling, mixing, and early characterizations of all NU-LHT-series members, save that of -5M.'

Caveat: the paper defines this as density 'at optimal packing', which may be closer to a maximum density than a loose bulk density. The curator should record that definition.

checks.notes: The extractor missed a schema field. It said no schema field fits the absolute density, but data-schema.md does have specific_gravity and density_g_cm3. Engelschion p.3 gives 'The absolute density measurements (volume measurement excluding pore space) of EAC-1, JSC-1A, JSC-2A, DNA and NU-LHT-3M resulted in 2.90, 2.92, 2.89, 2.79 and 3.08 g/cm3 respectively', so NU-LHT-3M = 3.08 is a candidate for specific_gravity/particle density. problems: The p.17 quote from the 2024 Lunar Simulant Assessment (JHU-APL, v1.0, March 31 2025) is verbatim.

R125's citation ('Lunar Simulants Assessment', with no year, DOI or URL) is ambiguous between the 2022 and 2024 reports. Only the 2024 report names the product in its body text. The 2022 report names 'NU-LHT-5M' only in its bibliography (the Rickman 2022 LPSC title), which I checked. Resolving R125 to the 2024 report is reasonable but should be recorded.

The 2024 report calls the product 'NUW-LHT-5M'. Treating that as the same product as the database's 'NU-LHT-5M' rests on Rickman 2024 p.6: 'Originally to be named NU-LHT-5M, the name has subsequently been changed to NUW-LHT-5M'.

The mention quote is not in the document. The abstract (PDF p.8) actually reads: 'A new simulant of the lunar highlands regolith, NUW-LHT-5M, was designed by NASA and manufactured by Washington Mills. The simulant was based on Apollo 16 data and is a member of the NU-LHT-series.' The extractor's version, 'designed by NASA and USGS as an improvement to the historical NU-LHT series', inserts USGS and changes the meaning. It even contradicts the extractor's own institution finding. A grep of the full text finds no sentence of that form.

The document is genuine (NASA/TP-20240007991, the local path is correct) and it does name the product. It should be re-added with a correct quote, for example p.6: 'Originally to be named NU-LHT-5M, the name has subsequently been changed to NUW-LHT-5M in recognition of the fabricator, including the glass: Washington Mills, Niagara Falls, NY.' The value checks below were judged against the document itself.

The quote is a bibliography entry (Rickman et al. 2022, LPSC abstract #1146, printed p.42) for a design abstract. It does not state a release date. I fetched and read that abstract: in 2022 it says 'Here we describe the design and efforts for the production of new highlands simulants' and 'Development of both simulants are now well advanced', so the simulant was not yet released.

Rickman 2024 records deliveries in 2023-2024: Table 4.4 note (4), 'Average of material delivered to ICON in 2023–2024', and Appendix H.1 dated July 24, 2023. No document supports 2022 as the release year.

The quote is verbatim at printed p.6, with an ellipsis. Stronger support nearby, also read in this session: p.6, 'It can also be provided in large quantities, on a continuous or sporadic basis with consistent quality controls'; Table 4.4 note (4), p.12, 'which is being used for the current production'. The 2024 Assessment p.3 lists 'USGS/NASA NUW-LHT-5M' among simulants from 'current providers'.
Verbatim at printed p.6. The abstract also says 'The simulant was based on Apollo 16 data'. The Slabic Guide p.22 has 'synthetic glass based on the average chemistry of the Apollo 16 soil samples'.
The claim that 'NASA / USGS' is unsupported is wrong: R125 (the 2024 Assessment) supports it.
Table 1 (p.5, checked on the rendered page) lists provider 'NASA/USGS' for 'NUW-LHT-5M | Highland with new compositionally accurate glass'.
p.3 says 'USGS/NASA NUW-LHT-5M' and p.10 says 'NUW-LHT-5M from USGS/NASA'.

There is a real conflict, and the curator should reconcile it. Rickman 2024 names Washington Mills as fabricator, and its Acknowledgments credit Wilson (USGS) with all NU-LHT members 'save that of -5M'. The 2022 LPSC abstract says 'Dr. Steve Wilson of the USGS, who made the existing simulant, has retired' and 'Washington Mills ... has agreed to collaborate with NASA'. 'NASA / Washington Mills' may be more accurate for production.

The extractor's paraphrase that NASA chose industry 'rather than continue with USGS (p.6)' is not in the text. p.6 says only 'This was in contrast with either the government making it, or a business creating a new product line.'

Verbatim at printed p.24 (Sec. 9). The quote leaves out that the sample was 'NUW-LHT-5M Test 1', an early production batch with lower Fe than the current product, tested at a low relative density of 1.265 g/cm3. The text notes that strength 'will only increase at higher relative densities'. Batch and density should be stored with the value.
Verbatim at p.24: 'ϕ = 30.69 ± 2.68°'. The same Test 1 and low-density caveat as for cohesion applies.

[1.264] Rickman Table 10.2, printed p.26: 'UCF NUW-LHT-5M 1.264' (minimum index density). The same table also gives 'Alfred (1) NUW-LHT-5M 1.25' (as received) and 'JSC NUW-LHT-5M 1.27 - 1.30'. There are several measurements, so this one should not stand alone as the product's single value.

[1.32] The value is printed ('NUW-LHT-5M (2) 1.32', note '(2) Baked per Wilkerson et al. (2023)'), but it was measured on material baked to 750 °C, not on the product as supplied. The extractor picked this baked value and left out the same lab's as-received value of 1.25. It should not be stored without the 'baked' qualifier.

Rickman Table 4.4, printed p.12, checked on the rendered image: 'WM NUW-LHT-5M (4) 26.79 14.08 0.01 4.31 - 6.35 0.05 0.08 0.01 47.83 0.52', with note (4) 'Average of material delivered to ICON in 2023–2024, which is being used for the current production.'

checks.notes:
The fabricated NEW1 mention quote is the main problem in this record.

The extractor also said the plain name 'NU-LHT-5M' is used only in passing. It missed the primary design document: Rickman, Shulman, Creedon & Effinger 2022, LPSC 53 abstract #1146, 'Design of NU-LHT-5M and -6M, Lunar Highland Simulants'. I fetched it from https://www.hou.usra.edu/meetings/lpsc2022/pdf/1146.pdf and saved it to papers/agent-fetched/Rickman_Shulman_Creedon_Effinger_2022_LPSC53_abs1146_Design_of_NU-LHT-5M_and_-6M_Lunar_Highland_Simulants.pdf. It uses the database's exact name throughout: 'new highlands simulants using natural analog materials (NU-LHT-5M)'. It should be added as a reference. It also says Washington Mills collaborates with NASA, that USGS's Wilson had retired, and that development was 'now well advanced' in 2022. Its Table 1 gives only the design glass target, not measured values.

The extractor missed another reference: the Slabic Guide p.22 names the product. 'NASA worked with Washington Mills ... Designated NUW-LHT-5M, this simulant contains Stillwater anorthosite and norite, a commercial olivine, and synthetic glass based on the average chemistry of the Apollo 16 soil samples (Rickman et al., 2024). The crystalline to glass ratio for NUW-LHT-5M is 60:40.' Slabic Table 25 (p.61) also has an NUW-LHT-5M crystalline-silica row.

Schema fields the extractor missed:
(a) glass_content_percent 40: Slabic p.22 '60:40'; the Rickman abstract says 'The other 40% of the simulant was a high calcium (An100), vesicular glass'.
(b) tons_produced_mt: Rickman p.6 'NASA has ordered 3.0 metric tons'; the abstract says 'already purchased 3 metric tons'.
(c) specific_gravity: Rickman p.25 He pycnometry, 'Values ranged between 2.81 and 2.838' (units misprinted as kg/m3; Table 10.1 gives 2824, 2813, 2838 and 2842 kg/m3). This is a range and needs human review.

Rickman 2024 characterizes several batches: Test 1, Test 2, and the WM current-production average. The shear data are from Test 1, the oxides from WM, and the QEMSCAN minerals probably from test material. The curator should decide which batch the database row represents. The extractor correctly used only the WM row for oxides.

I recommend renaming the product to 'NUW-LHT-5M', or storing that name as an alias, per Rickman p.6.

The mention quote is verbatim in the abstract on p.1; pdftotext splits it across lines by the Keywords column. The sample is the producer's product: 'The TLS- 01 soil sample from Space Zap Co. Ltd.' (Section 2.1.1, p.3). A byte-identical copy is at papers/LRS/DIRT project/files/1736/ (SHA-1 caa6dd64...).

The mention quote is verbatim in the abstract on p.1. The file name says 'Chancharoen et al.', but the first author is Siriluck. The paper also uses the misspellings 'TSL-01' and 'TLS-1' for the same product. A byte-identical copy is at papers/LRS/DIRT project/files/1809/ (SHA-1 36f27d9a...).

The unsupported verdict is correct. R052 Section 5, p.3 reads 'the TLS-01 cohesion value and friction angle is 0.066 ksc and 33.92 degree'. 0.066 ksc is about 6.47 kPa, not 4.9. Figure 2(b) on p.3 has no printed value, and its intercept is about 0.07 ksc. None of the 11 library documents that name TLS-01 contains a 4.9 near TLS. The later product TLS-01A does not match either: its abstract (Meesuay et al. 2023, OpenAlex record saved at papers/agent-fetched/OpenAlex_Meesuay2023_TLS-01A_JAerospEng_2026-09-24.json) gives 'friction angle and cohesion value were 29° and 3.05 kPa'. So 4.9 matches no document for TLS-01 or TLS-01A.

The unsupported verdict is correct. R052 gives 33.92 degree (Section 5, p.3), and a slope of about 0.67 in Figure 2(b) is consistent with that. The only 42.2 in the TLS-naming documents is an Apollo 12 SiO2 value in the 1793 review. TLS-01A gives 29°. 42.2 is unsupported.

The quote is verbatim in the NEW1 abstract on p.1. It is restated in Section 3.1.1, p.6: '54.55% polygonal shape ... and 45.45% bar shape'. Caveat: Jirasirichot measured both uncrushed and crushed TLS-01 (Figure 1 caption: 'uncrushed (A) and crushed (B)'), and Section 3.1.1 does not say which state the shape percentages refer to.

The words are verbatim in the NEW1 abstract, but they describe how the particles are distributed and dispersed in the SEM view, not ruggedness (surface roughness or angularity). Section 3.1.1 uses 'evenly distributed' about the particle size distribution: 'The particles were evenly distributed ( Figure 1) , as were the particle sizes of the simulated moon JSC-1A soil'. No opened document states a ruggedness value for TLS-01. The closest statement is R052 Discussion, p.3: 'it is possible that these actions resulted in a different particle shape (ie, rounded shape)', which is only a hypothesis. Mapping this phrase to ruggedness is a curator choice that the document does not support.

R052 p.1 reads 'Published: 1 July 2021'. The IGG-01 comparison table also has the row 'TLS-01 Thailand 2021 Basalt Mare geotechnical [34]', which is secondary. Conflict to note: Wikipedia (papers/agent-fetched/Wikipedia_Lunar_regolith_simulant_2026-09-22.html.txt) says 'In 2020, a team of independent researchers from Thailand also developed the Thailand Lunar Simulant - Batch 1 (TLS-1)'.

Ltd. was subjected to a physical examination', which shows the producer supplied the material to an outside university group. The analysis method is not stated. The values are verbatim, but the curator should review them before publishing.

checks.notes:
Checked by opening all three distinct documents (Seehanam 2021 = R052/R080; Jirasirichot 2023 = NEW1; Siriluck/Chancharoen/Seehanam 2021 biomining = NEW2), rendering R052 p.3 (Figure 2), and running a library-wide Python regex sweep of Sources_text. The shell grep wrapper and BSD grep -w returned nothing, so I did the sweep in Python. It finds exactly the 11 files the group lists as naming TLS-01: 7 copies of the three primary papers, plus the 1643 review (Liu et al. 2024), the 1757 IGG-01 paper (comparison table only), the 1793 review (country list only) and the Wikipedia capture. None of the 4 non-primary documents reports cohesion, friction angle or composition for TLS-01. The 1643 review's mineral row is labelled 'TLS-01A 60–75 10–20 5–10 15–20'. That is a different product and must not be used, as the extractor said.

The extractor's findings all check out. What it missed or should add:
(1) TLS-01A's own values, from its abstract (OpenAlex record fetched and saved at papers/agent-fetched/OpenAlex_Meesuay2023_TLS-01A_JAerospEng_2026-09-24.json), are 29° and 3.05 kPa. So the stored 4.9 and 42.2 are not TLS-01A values mislabelled as TLS-01; their origin is unknown. The TLS-01A abstract also says it was 'processed using simpler methods than the previously developed Thailand Lunar Simulant (TLS-01)', which confirms they are two separate products.
(2) The papers disagree on the feedstock location. R052 says 'collected from abandoned quarry beside Khereethan Dam, Chanthaburi province'; NEW2 says 'prepared from the basalt from Trad province'. The papers also prepare the material differently: R052 keeps the fraction 'finer than 15 millimeters', while NEW2 says 'sieved under a 100 mesh size'. NEW2's physical and mineral values may therefore describe a different batch or sieve fraction.
(3) Particle-size data exists but no field was proposed for it. R052 gives a <15 mm sieve cut. NEW2 gives <100 mesh. NEW1 Section 3.1.1 gives SEM particle dimensions: polygonal width 9.706–20.006 µm and length 12.941–35.212 µm; bar-shaped width 8.451–15.991 µm and length 10.183–29.985 µm. These are ranges for a human to judge; none is a d50.
(4) NEW1 also reports conductivity 'a conductivity of 0. 09 dS/ m' (p.7).
(5) I checked the element-basis EDX and XRF lists the extractor quoted in its notes (NEW1 p.6-7 and NEW2 Sections 2-3). They are verbatim and correctly attributed. The NEW2 figures 5.3% Fe, 3.03% Ca, etc. are for the evaporated leachate residue, not for TLS-01.
(6) Wikipedia dates development to 2020 and calls the product 'TLS-1'. The paper was published 1 July 2021.
(7) R080's DOI does not resolve (doi.org 404, Crossref not found). R080 should be merged with R052 and the DOI flagged as unregistered.

NEW1's own footnote source, the 2022 Lunar Simulants Assessment, separately states (of LHS-1D/LMS-1D collectively): 'Both dust simulants have a mean particle size of 7 microns' — close to but not identical to 9.34µm.

No document states LMS-1D's release year outright, but NEW1's reference list cites '[4] Exolith Lab (2021), LMS-1D Spec Sheet (Nov. 2021)', good circumstantial evidence a fact sheet for this product existed by November 2021, consistent with the stored 2021 release date.

No document literally states 'available'; inferred from the live storefronts (exolithsimulants.com lists 'Lunar Mare Dust (LMS-1D) Moon Dirt Simulant' as a current product, per a live fetch of that site done for sibling S095).
DS-S094 itself never states the company name; R129 (2022-era MIT paper) calls the producer 'Exolith Labs'.

results.notes: FeO is marked '–' (not reported) for LZS-1 in Table 2, so no oxide:FeO value could be extracted even though Fe2O3 is given; total of the LZS-1 oxide row is 99.6 wt%. Table 4 (SEM-EDX) gives plagioclase/pyroxene/olivine/metal-oxide ENDMEMBER compositions (e.g. An73.8Ab26.2Or0.0, Fo68.1) for four LZS-1 sample groups — these are mineral endmember chemistries, not modal (wt%/vol%) mineral abundances of the rock, so per the ground rules no mineral:<name> values were extracted; a curator wanting modal mineralogy will not find it in this paper. Physical-property values in Table 7 for porosity (26.0–34.0%) and UCS (4.1–92.9 MPa) are ranges with no corresponding schema field (no porosity/UCS scalar exists) so they were not added as new_values; likewise ultrasound pulse velocity (5105.9 m/s, Table 7) has no matching schema field. Density and porosity reported are of the intact BASALT ROCK (measured on cylindrical cores via mercury intrusion porosimetry), not of a crushed/loose regolith simulant powder — a curator should be aware bulk_density (loose material) is a different measurement not reported in this paper. NEW2 (CPESS-8 2025 abstract) is about a DIFFERENT, newer simulant called 'LuSIC-1' from La Palma (Canary Islands) developed by the Green Moon Project — NOT the same product as LZS-1 from Lanzarote/Tao quarry (IGEO, 2022); LZS-1 is only mentioned in passing there as a prior/comparison simulant used in germination tests ('consists of very fine particles that form a dusty consistency, making it difficult for root growth when wetted and causing the substrate to become compacted' — qualitative only, no quantifiable value, not added to new_values). A further library-sweep hit, papers/LRS/DIRT project/files/1793/S294992912500052X.html ('An overview on lunar regolith simulants solidification methods...', ScienceDirect, saved 2026), is a review that only lists 'Spain LZS-1' once in a country/simulant survey table with no LZS-1-specific data; per the review/usage-study exemption it was not opened in depth or added as a new_reference, just flagged here for the curator. composition_status is 'withheld_unverified' with an empty oxides/minerals list in the database, yet the primary paper (R099) does publish a full major-element oxide table for LZS-1 (Table 2) — this is the strongest single finding of this pass and is fully supported/quoted above; a curator should decide whether to lift the withheld status given this direct, on-topic source.

problems: Opened papers/LRS/s41598-022-20960-8.pdf. The other three listed copies have the same MD5 (e9710aa6fdf468ac27d27f78999652f0), so they are one document. The title on p.1 reads 'LZS-1, Lanzarote (Canary Island, Spain) lunar (Apollo 14) basaltic soil simulant' (the hyphen is a non-breaking hyphen), which matches the quote. p.1 also says 'In this sense, a new lunar simulant, LZS-1, has been developed in Spain.'

The mention is real. Table 1 ('Summary of lunar regolith simulants in various countries and regions') in the stripped HTML reads 'Australia 1 ALRS-1 [68] Thailand 1 TLS-01/01A [69] Spain 1 LZS-1 [70] Turkey 1 TBG-1 [71]'. The extractor's quote adds a ' , ' after [69] that is not in the text. Bibliography entry [70] is Alberquilla et al., Sci Rep 12 (1) (2022), p. 16470.
The metadata is wrong. The year is 2024, not 2025: the page reads 'International Journal of Mining Science and Technology Volume 34, Issue 10, October 2024, Pages 1341-1363'.
The authors are known, not 'unspecified': 'Bo Liu, Peng Sun, Wei Yao, Tao Li, Wei Xu'. The DOI is https://doi.org/10.1016/j.ijmst.2024.09.005.
The table sits just before section '2.1. Physical and mechanical properties', not inside it.
This is a review that only lists the name. It gives no LZS-1 data.

Opened papers/agent-fetched/CPESS-8_2025_Alberquilla_MIT_GreenMoon_LUSIC-1_abstract.pdf. The quote is verbatim: 'To achieve this milestone, germination experiments were tested in other lunar simulant LZS-1 (developed at IGEO in 2022), where toxic elements and nutritional deficiencies negatively impacted crop growth.'

It is a conference abstract (CPESS 8, Malaga, 26-30 May 2025), not a report. Its subject is LuSIC-1, a different simulant from La Palma. LZS-1 appears only as the earlier simulant used in the germination tests.
The quote 'germination experiments were tested in other lunar simulant LZS-1 (developed at IGEO in 2022)' is in the NEW2 abstract body.
R099 corroborates it. p.10 has 'Received: 8 February 2022; Accepted: 21 September 2022', and the rendered page also shows 'Published online: 01 October 2022'.

I agree the value is unsupported. I searched R099, NEW1, NEW2, the Chen et al. 2025 review (files/1793) and the two other CPESS-8 abstracts in agent-fetched. None says whether the LZS-1 material is available.

R099's closing lines are publisher boilerplate: p.10 'All datasets used and/or analyses carried out and results obtained are available from the corresponding author on reasonable request.' and p.11 'Correspondence and requests for materials should be addressed to F.A.' Neither is an availability status for the material.
R099 p.5 says only 1500 g were produced: 'The rest (2/3) was taken to a ball mill where 1500 g of regolith simulant were obtained.' That points to a very small batch, not ongoing supply.
R099 p.5 prints 'LZS-1 is similar to CAS-1, JSC-1 and to the Apollo 14 agglutinate sample 14163' with reference superscript 5 after 14163. The extractor's quote drops the superscript, which is fine.
The Table 2 caption on p.6 includes 'Data of Apollo 14* and 14163* were cited from Heiken et al. (1991)'.
The Conclusions on p.10 add 'A new basaltic simulant from Lanzarote has been developed, which matches with the Apollo 14 lunar soil.'
The p.1 affiliation footnote 1 reads 'Instituto de Geociencias (CSIC, UCM), Calle del Dr. Severo Ochoa, 7, 28040 Madrid, Spain.'
The p.10 Data availability section reads 'Agreement between the Institute of Geosciences (IGEO) and the Cabildo Insular de Lanzarote'.
The can labels in Fig. 4 on p.4 also show the IGEO logo.
The value is right but the page is wrong: Table 2 is on p.6, not p.5 (checked on the rendered page).
The row reads 'LZS-1 45.6 2.7 12.3 0.2 8.2 10.6 14.6 – 2.9 0.7 2.0 99.6', and the column order in the extractor's quote matches the table.
The analysis was XRF on 10 g of crushed Tao basalt (p.5).
The value 2.7 is right. Table 2 is on p.6, not p.5.
The value 12.3 is right. Table 2 is on p.6, not p.5.
The value 0.2 is right. Table 2 is on p.6, not p.5.
The value 8.2 is right. Table 2 is on p.6, not p.5.

The value 14.6 is right. Table 2 is on p.6, not p.5. FeO is printed as '–' for LZS-1, so 14.6 is presumably total iron expressed as Fe2O3.
The value 2.9 is right. Table 2 is on p.6, not p.5.
The value 0.7 is right. Table 2 is on p.6, not p.5.
The value 2.0 is right. Table 2 is on p.6, not p.5.
Table 1 is on p.4, not p.3. Its rows are 'LZS-1 (A) 63–125' and 'LZS-1 (B) < 63' under 'Particle size (µm)'.

These are the two sieve cuts the product is supplied in, not a measured distribution. p.2 gives the masses: 'One belongs to the fraction between 63–125 µm (1000 g) and the other represents the fraction < 63 µm (500 g).'

The paper is inconsistent about the cut. The Fig. 4 can labels read '125-65 µm size fraction' and '<65 µm size fraction', and p.5 says fines were passed through 'a No. 230 (0.065 mm) sieve'. A curator should know about this.
Table 7 is on p.10, not p.9. Its row reads 'Density (g/cm3) 2.9–3.0 | 2.4–2.5 | 2.8–3.0', and the LZS-1 column is 2.8–3.0. The value is a range, so it must go to human review.

The p.9 text says 'Density values ranged from 2.8 g/cm3 to 3.0 g/cm3 in all Tao samples.' This was measured by mercury intrusion porosimetry on cylindrical cores of the feedstock basalt (samples labelled 'LZS-1r').

Table 6 on p.10 separates real density (3.0 and 2.8) from apparent density (2.0 and 2.0). So 2.8–3.0 is the real (skeletal) density of the rock, closer in meaning to specific gravity than to a density of the powder.

checks.notes:
All three references and all stored and new values held up on reopening. The main corrections are to locations: Table 1 is on p.4, Table 2 on p.6 and Table 7 on p.10 (the extractor gave p.3, p.5 and p.9). NEW1's year and authors are also wrong (2024, Bo Liu et al., DOI 10.1016/j.ijmst.2024.09.005).

The extractor missed two values:
1. particle_morphology: R099 p.5 says 'With regards to the grain shapes, there are mainly angular (irregular) (Fig. 5)'. This is a supported qualitative value.
2. tons_produced_mt: R099 p.5 says '1500 g of regolith simulant were obtained', and p.2 gives '63–125 µm (1000 g)' and '< 63 µm (500 g)'. That is about 0.0015 t, but the paper gives grams, so it should go to human review rather than become a number.

Other content in R099 that has no schema field:
- Table 3 on p.6 lists LZS-1 trace elements by ICP-MS (for example 'Sr 1332.43', 'Cr 691.37', 'Ni 459.07'). No units are printed.
- Table 5 on p.9 gives ultrasound velocities for LZS-1r cores (5271.41, 5594.81, 4740.29 and 4817.24 m/s).
- Table 6 on p.10 gives mercury porosity (34.1 and 26.1 %) and apparent density 2.0.
- Table 7 gives porosity '26.0–34.0', UCS '4.1–92.9' and ultrasound pulse velocity '5105.9'.
- p.5 says vesicles 'can reach 48% of the total'.
All of these were measured on intact rock, not on the powder.

Mineralogy is present but not quantified, so there are no mineral values. p.5 names olivine, clino/ortho pyroxene, calcic plagioclase, glass, and 'metal oxides mainly of iron, titanium, and chromium'. The Fig. 7 XRD shows only peak labels (Ol, Px, Plag). p.6 says 'No carbonates, quartz or clay have been found'. Table 4 gives SEM-EDX endmember compositions (for example An73.8Ab26.2Or0.0 and Fo68.1), not modal abundances. The extractor is right to leave these out.

p.2 says 'we manufacture the low titanium regolithic simulant', which bears on type (Mare).

Library sweep: grep for 'LZS-1', 'LZS1' and 'LZS 1' in Sources_text found only the 7 known files. They are the four identical R099 copies, NEW1, NEW2 and papers/LRS/DIRT project/files/1793/S294992912500052X.html. That last one is Chen et al., Biogeotechnics, 'Available online 25 October 2025', DOI 10.1016/j.bgtech.2025.100212. It is a review whose country table lists only 'Spain LZS-1' and gives no data. The extractor called it 'saved 2026', but the page says online 25 October 2025.

The two other CPESS-8 Alberquilla abstracts in agent-fetched (LuSIC-1 methodology and PaLMALab) do not mention LZS-1. A NotebookLM capture of Chen et al. 2025 under papers/LRS/Sources also names LZS-1, but it is the same review. The only other hits are the project's own Global Registry and dashboard pages, which are not evidence and were not used.

NEW2 describes the dusty, compacting behaviour of 'the lunar simulant', which appears to be LZS-1. It gives no numbers.

I agree with the extractor that composition_status 'withheld_unverified' conflicts with the full LZS-1 oxide row in R099 Table 2.

results.notes: TBG-1 = simulant 'S07' in Toklu et al. 2023 (NEW1): the Jaya-algorithm optimized blend of 14 local Turkish feedstock rock/soil samples (labelled A1, P1, E1, G1, K1, S1, T1, U1, UR, AB, KB, OL, UK, IL) whose oxide profile gave the smallest discrepancy (d=10.00, best of 18 Apollo targets) to Apollo 14 soil R07. Its full oxide composition (wt%) is in Table 1, added under new_values. This is the paper's computed/target-fit composition from an optimization procedure matching oxide percentages, not a stated independent XRF/XRD measurement of the finished physical TBG-1 batch — worth flagging given composition_status='withheld_unverified'. Table 4 of the same paper gives XRD mineral phases per FEEDSTOCK sample (e.g. OL: Forsterite/Enstatite/Lizardite; IL: Ilmenite/Rutile/Quartz; K1: Augite/Nepheline/Leucite/Indialite/Muscovite/Pargasite/Amorphous; etc.) — these are the blended ingredients' mineralogy, not TBG-1's own mineral composition, so per the composition rule none are reported as mineral: values; the paper gives no quantified mineral composition for the finished TBG-1 blend itself. Unsalan et al. 2024 (NEW2, only its abstract was accessible) adds a qualitative note that Raman spectroscopy on TBG-1 implies it is 'mainly forsteritic olivine' and that TBG-1's (Mg,Ca)/Al2O3 ratio resembles lunar highland impact glass while its Al2O3/TiO2 resemble Apollo 11 soil — all unquantified, so not entered as values. Two of the six listed documents (1711 = LSS-ISAC-1 ResearchGate page, 1765 = TJ-1 ResearchGate page) do not discuss TBG-1 in their own body text at all: the TBG-1 sentence in both is the identical NEW2 abstract snippet shown as a ResearchGate 'Recommended publications' sidebar item, not content of the LSS-ISAC-1 or TJ-1 papers themselves — I still marked names_simulant=true because the sentence genuinely names and describes TBG-1, but the real source is NEW2, cited accordingly. Possible discrepancy for the curator: Ruan et al. 2024 (NEW3) classifies TBG-1's Type as 'Mare', while Toklu et al. 2023 places its target Apollo-14 samples R05–R07 in a 'mixed' mare/highland zone, not purely mare (no scalar field exists in this group file to record this, so no value/new_value entry was made for it). Library sweep: grep -rliw for 'TBG-1', 'TBG1', and 'TBG' across Sources_text returned exactly the same 6 files already listed for this simulant; no additional library documents name TBG-1. No weak candidates (library_documents_possibly_naming_it) were listed for this simulant.

I searched all six documents and found no statement about production, sale or availability of TBG-1. The only 'available' near TBG-1 is ResearchGate's 'Full-text available' label. results.notes: MAJOR FINDING — likely duplicate/misattributed simulant: R022 (Taylor et al. 2008, 'Jurassic Diabase from Leesburg, VA: A Proposed Lunar Simulant', NLSI Lunar Science Conference abstract #2054) had no local_path/doi/url in the database, so it was located via web search and fetched from https://www.lpi.usra.edu/meetings/nlsc2008/pdf/2054.pdf (confirmed against NASA NTRS 20080023350: same title/authors/venue/year), and saved to Sources/papers/agent-fetched/Taylor_et_al_2008_NLSI2054_GSC-1_Jurassic_diabase_Leesburg.pdf. Read in full, this abstract calls the material 'GSC-1' throughout ('this rock, GSC-1 henceforth') and never once writes 'GCA-1'. Yet at least four other documents (Taylor et al. 2016 Table 2; the LEAG-CAPTEM report Appendix 4; the IGG-01 (2024) Table 1; and a ResearchGate-embedded citation excerpt) cite this exact same 2008 reference while calling the product 'GCA-1'. The NASA ARES simulants page even writes the pair as 'GSC-1 (GCA-1)', treating them as one product. This strongly suggests 'GCA-1' is a recurring transcription/citation variant of 'GSC-1' rather than a truly distinct simulant, and that S023 (GCA-1) and S117 (GSC-1) may be duplicate database entries for the same real material. Because R022's own text never says 'GCA-1', it is marked names_simulant=false above and its detailed modal mineral composition (plagioclase 45%, clinopyroxene 45%, magnetite 5%, quartz 3%, biotite 2%) is reported instead under S117/GSC-1, per the exact-product rule. Recommend the curator investigate merging these two entries and reassign R022 to S117. Additionally: IGG-01's Table 1 gives GCA-1's source material as 'Diabase' — this is the parent feedstock rock, not a mineral-composition breakdown, so it is not reported as a mineral: value; no oxide or mineral percentages for a document explicitly labelled 'GCA-1' were found in any opened source.

results.notes: CRITICAL NAME-MATCH ISSUE: no document in the library or on Space Resource Technologies' current website uses the exact string 'LHD-1D' except R131 (JHU-APL 2024 Lunar Simulant Assessment), which uses it repeatedly (Introduction p.10, Table 2 p.11, Results pp.19/30). Space Resource Technologies' current catalog and datasheets instead use 'LHS-1D' (Lunar Highlands Dust Simulant) for what appears, on every measurable point, to be the SAME product: (1) identical phrase 'Reference Material: Average lunar highlands' (matches the stored lunar_sample_reference verbatim); (2) same description as an extra-fine, ball-milled dust variant of LHS-1 in the tens-of-microns range (R131: 'particle sizes up to 35 µm'; SRT page: 'particles finer than 30 µm, mean ~7 µm'; Millwater et al. 2022: '<30µm... mean particle size of 7µm'); (3) near-identical feedstock/mineral breakdown (R131: 74% anorthosite/24% basaltic cinder/<0.5% each ilmenite,olivine,bronzite; SRT datasheet: 74.4/24.7/0.4/0.2/0.3; Millwater et al. 2022 Table 1: 74.4/24.7/0.4/0.3(Olivine)/0.2(Pyroxene) — minor 0.2/0.3 swap between the two independent SRT-affiliated sources, otherwise matching); (4) I searched SRT's full current catalog (fetched 2026-09-24): zero occurrences of 'LHD-1D', 11 of 'LHS-1D'. Most likely explanation: 'LHD-1D' is a letter transposition of 'LHS-1D' (S/D swapped), introduced either by the JHUAPL report or upstream in this database's pipeline. Because of this, I have NOT marked the LHS-1D-sourced data as 'supported' for the stored fields (those documents literally name a different string) — instead the full matching dataset (bulk density, particle size, geotechnical properties, full oxide suite, 3 minor minerals) is placed in new_values, clearly tagged to the LHS-1D-named sources, for a human curator to decide: (a) rename this simulant to 'LHS-1D' and accept the new_values, (b) keep 'LHD-1D' as a distinct/legacy designation with only R131's composition-percentage row as its source, or (c) merge with an 'LHS-1D' record elsewhere in the DB if one exists. Separately: '74% anorthosite / 24% basaltic cinder' (both in R131 and the LHS-1D datasheet) is FEEDSTOCK BLEND, not modal mineralogy, and per project convention must NOT be stored as mineral:Anorthosite / mineral:'Glass-rich basalt' values — only the minor Ilmenite/Olivine/Bronzite figures (all <0.5 wt%, individually quantified, not merely 'trace') are genuine candidate mineral values, included above. R131's own reference record has local_path=null despite the exact file existing at papers/LRS/2024_Lunar_Simulant_Assessment_Report.pdf; recommend populating it.

values.note: R109 does not name a product called 'FROST-Y' — it is a general study of icy-regolith production built on the dry base simulant LHS-1. It reports overall bulk densities of 0.87±0.33 g/mL (Proc 1 average) and 0.90±0.12 g/mL (Proc 2 average); Table 3's six individual sample measurements range 0.78-0.97 g/mL, of which two (Proc 2, samples 2 & 3) happen to read '0.89'. This is not a single per-product specification value, just two of six individual lab measurements in a process-development study. Dry base LHS-1 itself has bulk density 1.40 g/cm3 (its own datasheet) — a very different figure. No document anywhere in the library gives a bulk density explicitly labelled for a product named 'FROST-Y'.

Not stated for an icy/FROST-Y variant anywhere. The dry base simulant LHS-1 has particle size range '<0.04 µm – 1000 µm' per its own datasheet (matching the upper bound stored here), but R109 never repeats or confirms this for the icy product, and no document names a range specifically for 'FROST-Y'.

'FROST-Y' is absent from Space Resource Technologies' current online catalog (checked 2026-09-24: 0 occurrences). R109 describes only a laboratory production method/experiment, not a marketed, orderable product.

values.quote: The Artemis program plans to take astronauts to the lunar south pole, where surface properties might be very different from equatorial regions previously visited by Apollo astronauts
values.note: No document states 'Lunar South Pole' as FROST-Y's compositional reference. R109 frames its icy-regolith work around Artemis's south-pole PSR targets, which plausibly explains the field's choice, but FROST-Y is built on the lunar-HIGHLANDS base LHS-1 (Cannon & Britt 2019 call it 'a frozen volatile-bearing highlands simulant'), not a south-pole compositional analog. Likely a mission-context label rather than a true reference-material statement; worth curator review.

Documents that discuss the underlying work (Cannon & Britt 2019; Šļumba et al. 2024/R109) attribute it to 'University of Central Florida' / 'Exolith Lab, Oviedo, FL', not 'Space Resource Technologies'. Per the 2024 JHU-APL report (used elsewhere in this group), Space Resource Technologies is '(previously Exolith)' — the same org, rebranded — so this is plausible but not directly confirmed for FROST-Y specifically, and FROST-Y does not appear in SRT's current catalog at all.

results.notes: FROST-Y is named (exactly) only in Cannon & Britt (2019), a one-page conference abstract with no quantitative data — the ONLY document in the entire library using this exact product name. R109, the group file's assigned reference, matches title and DOI exactly but is a different kind of document: a full study ('Development of icy regolith simulant for lunar permanently shadowed regions', Šļumba, Sargeant & Britt, 2024) describing a variable production METHOD (Proc 1 vs Proc 2, with sample-to-sample variance) built on LHS-1, not a fixed per-product datasheet, and it never uses the string 'FROST-Y'. It is plausible this method produced (or evolved into) FROST-Y, but the paper does not make that connection explicit, so none of the stored scalars can be marked 'supported' by it. I read R109 via the NotebookLM text capture at papers/LRS/Sources/Slumbaetal.2024PSRIcySimulant.pdf.html (permitted per project convention for reading) but cite it via its existing DOI (10.1016/j.asr.2024.01.014), already present in the reference record; no PDF of this ScienceDirect article was found elsewhere in the local library. No oxide/mineral composition exists anywhere in the library for FROST-Y, consistent with composition_status='not_extracted'. Library sweep for 'FROST-Y' (with and without the hyphen) found no further documents beyond Cannon & Britt (2019).

The quotes are verbatim on the saved LHS-1D product page (title and 'The simulant consists exclusively of particles finer than 30 µm, with a mean particle size of approximately 7 µm'), with '"available":true'. The page names LHS-1D, never LHD-1D. That it is the same product is the extractor's inference, not stated anywhere.

datasheets/SRT/LHS-1D_spec_Dec2025.pdf p.1 reads 'Simulant Name: LHS-1D Dust Simulant' and 'Reference Material: Average lunar highlands' (doc 003-03-001-1225). It names LHS-1D, not LHD-1D, so it attaches to S096 only if the curator accepts that they are the same product.

Verified in the catalog capture: 'Lunar Highlands Dust (LHS-1D)' is present, with 0 'LHD-1D', 0 'DUST-Y' and 0 'FROST-Y'. The document does not name LHD-1D. It is evidence that the name is absent, not a reference naming this product.

Millwater et al. 2022 LPSC 53 #2038 p.1 has the quote verbatim ('LHS-1D has the same mineralogy as LHS-1, but is ball milled for 24-48 hours producing a particle size of <30µm with a mean particle size of 7µm'). It names LHS-1D, not LHD-1D. Its reference [2] is 'Exolith Lab (2021), LHS-1D Spec Sheet (Nov. 2021)'.

Unsupported is correct. The cited sentence is on R131 p.3 (Introduction), not p.10. It shows LHD-1D was new to that study, not when it was released. If LHD-1D is LHS-1D, the date is contradicted: the SRT products JSON gives the LHS-1D listing created_at 2020-11-25, and Millwater cites a Nov. 2021 LHS-1D spec sheet.
Unsupported under the exact name is correct. R131 only says '4 simulants from 2 current providers', and 'LHD-1D' is absent from the SRT catalog and products JSON.
R131's LHD-1D representation is 'Dust variant, particle sizes up to 35 µm'. 'Average lunar highlands' appears only on the LHS-1D and LHS-1 datasheets.

checks.notes: Library sweep: 'LHD-1D' appears only in the 2024 JHUAPL report, and there are no hits for 'LHD1D'. R131's Table 2 row for LHD-1D uses the same minor components as the current SRT LHS-1 and LHS-1D sheets (ilmenite, olivine, bronzite). Its LHS-1 row instead lists 'basalt, ilmenite, pyroxene, and olivine'. The current SRT products JSON has 'Lunar Highlands Dust Simulant (LHS-1D)', created 2020-11-25 and available=True, and nothing called LHD-1D. That strongly suggests LHD-1D is a typo for LHS-1D, but no document says so. The curator should decide before anything from the LHS-1D sources is attached to S096. If S096 is merged into an LHS-1D record, release_date=2024 is also wrong, since the product existed by Nov 2020/2021. The 74% anorthosite / 24% basaltic cinder split (R131) and 74.4/24.7 (datasheet) is a feedstock blend, notes only. R131 needs local_path papers/LRS/2024_Lunar_Simulant_Assessment_Report.pdf. The 'previously Exolith' statement is on R131 p.3.

problems: R109 does not name FROST-Y. The abstract quote is verbatim ('We present a new production method for lunar permanently shadowed regions (PSRs) icy regolith simulant. We build on an existing lunar highlands simulant, by adapting it for lunar poles'). The extractor's note is wrong that no PDF is in the library. papers/LRS/Slumbaetal.2024PSRIcySimulant.pdf is the full Advances in Space Research 73 (2024) 3222–3234 article, and I read it. Recommend setting it as R109's local_path.
Cannon & Britt 2019 p.1: '...a frozen volatile-/bearing highlands simulant (FROST-Y)...' (wrapped). There is no quantitative data. This is the only document in the library that names FROST-Y.

Unsupported is correct. R109 Table 3 (p.3231) has 0.89 g/mL only for 'Proc 2 (2)' and 'Proc 2 (3)', out of six batches ranging 0.78–0.97. The p.3230 text gives averages 'which is 0:87  0:33g=mL and' / '0:90  0:12g=mL for Proc 1 and Proc 2 respectively' (± lost in extraction). No document names FROST-Y.

The extractor's note is factually wrong that R109 'never repeats or confirms this for the icy product'. R109 Section 2.2, p.3227, says 'The sieved icy regolith therefore has a grain size / of < 1 mm, and does not account for potential icy regolith / containing larger ice grains.' That matches the stored '<1000 µm'. It counts as support only if R109's icy simulant is FROST-Y, which R109 never says. The status depends on the curator's identity decision.

Unsupported is correct and is actually contradicted. R109 p.3223 says a PSR-simulant user has 'to manufacture their / own simulant as it is not a readily available product.' FROST-Y is absent from the SRT catalog and products JSON (0 occurrences).

The Introduction quote on p.3222 is verbatim (wrapped) and is mission context only. R109 p.3224: 'Lunar polar regions are dominated by / lunar highlands type regolith' and 'we use Lunar Highlands / Simulant (LHS-1) ... as the base for / the PSR simulant.' Cannon & Britt call FROST-Y 'highlands'. There is no south-pole reference material.

Unsupported under a strict reading. R109 p.3224: 'The simulant is made by Exolith Lab' (about the LHS-1 base), and the affiliation is 'Exolith Lab, 532 South Econ Cir, Oviedo, FL'. Linking to SRT needs R131 p.3 'Space Resource Technologies (previously Exolith)'. It is plausible but inferred.

checks.notes: Library sweep: 'FROST-Y', 'FROSTY' and 'Frost-Y' appear only in the two Cannon & Britt 2019 copies. R109's local PDF (papers/LRS/Slumbaetal.2024PSRIcySimulant.pdf) exists and should become R109's local_path. The extractor missed R109's '< 1 mm' grain-size statement and its 'not a readily available product' statement, which argues against availability=Available. Whether R109's icy simulant is FROST-Y is not established by any document. If the curator links them, particle_size_distribution '<1 mm' (p.3227) is supported, but bulk_density 0.89 is still not a product value (the averages are 0.87±0.33 and 0.90±0.12 g/mL). results.notes: MAJOR FINDING — likely EAC-1A→EAC-1 misattribution: Engelschiøn et al. 2020 (NEW1) explicitly states its own naming convention (p.1): grain-size-dependent physical properties (bulk density, cohesion, angle of repose, sphericity) of the processed dusty material are labelled 'EAC-1A'; only non-grain-size-dependent chemical/mineralogical data on the parent quarried basanite rock are labelled 'EAC-1'. The database's stored bulk_density=1.45 and cohesion=0.38 for EAC-1 are, verbatim, the paper's EAC-1A figures (p.3), not EAC-1 figures — analogous to citing JSC-1A data for JSC-1AC. No opened document (including Zemeny et al. 2024, NEW2) gives a single-value bulk density or any cohesion figure for EAC-1 itself. Recommend the curator either drop these two stored values for EAC-1 or reassign them to an EAC-1A record. Citation R017 also has an author mismatch: the stored citation lists 'Manick, Gill, Mason, Crowther' but the only 49th LPSC 2018 abstract in the library with a matching title (papers/LRS/1411.pdf) is authored by Manick, Gill, Najorka, Smith, Duvet — no paper by Mason/Crowther on this topic was found anywhere in the library (grep -rliw "Crowther" only hits an unrelated LHS document); likely a data-entry error in the reference. Composition_status is 'withheld_unverified' but rich, exact-product composition data does exist and is publicly citable: Nieke et al. 2019 (NEW3, via Schleppi et al. 2018 supplier spec) gives a full 10-oxide table for EAC-1, and Zemeny et al. 2024 (NEW2) gives quantified modal mineralogy (AMICS SEM-EDS, 12 phases) — none of this was previously in the DB (oxides/minerals were both empty). Cross-document composition discrepancies for the curator to weigh: SiO2 43.7 (Engelschiøn/Nieke) vs 42.1-42.3 (Zemeny XRF/ICP range); MgO 11.9/11.90 (Engelschiøn/Nieke) vs 13.1-13.8 (Zemeny range); TiO2 2.4/2.40 (Engelschiøn/Nieke) vs 2.1 (Zemeny) — likely reflect different EAC-1 batches/years (supplier spec vs 2017 Engelschiøn batch vs June-2023 Zemeny batch) rather than error. Also 'Olivine' has two non-reconcilable values: 15.37% (Zemeny, AMICS-measured modal %) vs 13.88% (Engelschiøn Supplementary Table 1, a computational normative estimate from bulk chemistry, explicitly NOT a direct measurement) — kept as separate entries, human should decide which (if either) to store. EAC-1 is a single quarried basanite rock (Siebengebirge Volcanic Field, Königswinter, Germany — Manick's abstract calls the same locality 'the Eifel region'), not a blend of feedstocks, so no blend-ratio caveat applies. LIBRARY SWEEP — documents that merely mention EAC-1 in passing (comparison tables/reviews/usage studies), not opened for data: papers/Linke_etal_2020_TUBS-M_TUBS-T_modular_Regolith_Simulant_System_PlanetSpaceSci_180_104747.pdf; papers/LRS/1-s2.0-S0094576525001109-main.pdf; papers/LRS/DIRT project/files/1643/S2095268624001381.html; papers/LRS/DIRT project/files/1793/S294992912500052X.html; papers/LRS/DIRT project/files/1712/330911730_The_Preparation_and_Characterization_of_NEU-1_Lunar_Soil_Simulants.html; papers/agent-fetched/Linke_etal_2022_Geotechnical_Shear_Behavior_TUBS-M_TUBS-T_TUBS-I_Materials_15_8561_PMC9737658.html; papers/agent-fetched/ISECG_2021_ISRU_Technology_Gap_Assessment_Report_Apr2021.pdf (mentions EAC-1 only in equipment/facility tables, no composition data). papers/LRS/DIRT project/files/1765/276962935_Properties_of_TJ-1_Lunar_Soil_Simulant.html is a ResearchGate paywalled stub for an unrelated 2012 TJ-1 paper; its only 'EAC-1' text is an unrelated 'recommended reading' sidebar snippet for a different (inaccessible) paper, not usable. papers/LRS/DIRT project/files/1668/S2666539521000043.html led to discovering NEW3 (Nieke et al. 2019) via its bibliography and was opened for that purpose. papers/LRS/Figueira - Fungal Biomining of Lunar Regolith simulant EAC-1A.pdf and papers/LRS/Ginés-Palomares et al. - 2023 - Laser melting manufacturing of large elements of l.pdf are primarily about EAC-1A (a distinct, derived product); Ginés-Palomares does restate EAC-1's absolute density as 2.9 g/cm3 but explicitly as a citation of Engelschiøn et al. 2020 (NEW1), not an independent measurement, so it was not added as a separate reference.

Zemeny 2024 Table 2 (p.15, not p.16) gives EAC-1 loose 1.46 and tapped 1.98 g/cm3, and min–max dry unit weight 1.56–2.25 g/cm3. Zemeny's text on p.13 says 'loose and tapped bulk densities between 1.46 and 1.99 g/cm³', which is internally inconsistent with Table 2.
In Zemeny Table 2 the value 1.45 appears only as Lumina250's tapped bulk density.

'Unsupported for EAC-1' is correct. Engelschiøn p.3: 'The cohesion of EAC-1A at a density of 1.95 g/cm3 was estimated to be 0.38 kPa'. The value belongs to EAC-1A, and the paper says the density–cohesion relation could not be established.
Zemeny 2024, Manick 2018, Nieke 2019 and the swept documents give no cohesion for EAC-1.

Verbatim in Ruan et al. 2024, Table 1, p.149: 'EAC-1/1A Germany 2017; 2020'. Assigning 2017 to EAC-1 and 2020 to EAC-1A is an inference from the paired notation, which the table also uses for 'DNA-1/1A Italy 2014; 2019'.

This is a secondary compilation citing Engelschiøn 2020, and Engelschiøn itself states no release year. Indirect support: Manick 2018 says EAC-1 grain-size work was 'carried out in mid-late 2017', and its sub-sample IDs are '17DE01, 17DE02, 17DE03'. Manick also cites 'Nash et al. (2017) EPSC 2017-463' for EAC-1; that source is not in the library.
A human should confirm this value against a primary dated source.
'Unsupported' is correct: no document states 'Available (Research)'.

The extractor overstates Manick: it says three batches were 'acquired by the Curation Facility' as voucher specimens, not that EAC-1 is distributed. Engelschiøn p.6 'stored and curated by the ESA Sample Analogue Curation facility at ECSAT, UK' is said of 'the material' in an EAC-1A context.

Patzwald et al. 2025 (papers/LRS/1-s2.0-S0094576525001109-main.pdf) describes European simulants including 'EAC-1(A)' as 'only partially characterised and available'. That is not a clean availability statement.

'Unsupported' is correct: no document calls EAC-1 'Low-Ti'. Some documents lean the other way. Zemeny p.8 describes EAC-1 as having 'further high TiO2 (2.1 wt%)', though relative to the highland Lumina samples. Ruan Table 1 types EAC-1/1A as just 'Mare'. Zanotti et al. (NotebookLM capture 'Planetary Soil Simulant Characterisation_ NU-L.html') lists 'EAC-1 Mixed (Apollo 17)'.

checks.notes:
All six group documents opened. The three Engelschiøn PDF copies are identical, as are the two Manick 1411 copies. I independently confirmed the extractor's main finding: the stored bulk_density 1.45 and cohesion 0.38 for EAC-1 are Engelschiøn's EAC-1A figures (p.3), and no document gives either value for EAC-1.

To verify NEW3 against the original rather than the NotebookLM capture, I fetched the Nieke et al. 2019 full text from Europe PMC. It is saved at papers/agent-fetched/Nieke_etal_2019_Dense_Thick_Films_EAC-1_Materials_12_487_PMC6384728.xml; use it as NEW3's local_path.

Location errors (quotes are otherwise correct):
- NEW2 mention: p.2, not p.1.
- Zemeny 'reported to be a mare simulant': p.13, not p.12.
- Zemeny Table 1: p.3.
- Zemeny Table 2: p.15, not p.16.
- Nieke Table 1: p.3, not p.5.

The extractor's 'kind' labels are wrong for all four new references: NEW1 and NEW2 are primary research, NEW3 is a research communication, and NEW4 is a research article with a secondary compilation table.

Values the extractor missed, all for EAC-1:
- Zemeny 2024 (June-2023 batch):
  - SAT abrasivity 'EAC-1 represents low abrasiveness (6.5)' (p.7).
  - Min/max dry unit weight '15.36 and 22.17 kN/m3' (p.7).
  - Water content: 'EAC-1 suggests no water content' (p.7).
  - Table 2 (p.15): min–max dry unit weight 1.56–2.25 g/cm3; loose bulk density 1.46 and tapped 1.98 g/cm3. The text on p.13 says 1.46–1.99, so the paper is inconsistent.
  - Mineralogic SEM-EDS wt% (p.13): anorthite 12.6, andesine 6.3, anorthoclase 6.0, titanomagnetite 6.7, quartz 1.5, augite 31.3, olivine 15.1; basaltic glass, mica and clay 5.6–5.7 each. These conflict with the AMICS area-% set the extractor proposed, so a human must choose one method.
  - XRD (p.11): plagioclase 'appears to be andesine (An50)', plus an amorphous phase; values are in Supplementary Table S8, which is not in the library.
- Engelschiøn Supplementary Tables 2 and 3: thin-section vol% for two host-rock units.
  - OP-1: plagioclase 64, olivine 25, pyroxene 5, amphibole 0.5, quartz 0.5, opaque 5.
  - OR-1: plagioclase 54, olivine 29, pyroxene 10, quartz 2, amphibole 2, opaque 5.
  - Two unit-level measurements, so a human should review them rather than store one.
- Engelschiøn sphericity 0.601 and 0.591 (p.3) belongs to the 0.2–0.5 mm and 0.5–1 mm sieve fractions, which are different products; do not store it for EAC-1.

Primary source not in the library: Chen et al. 2025 (papers/LRS/DIRT project/files/1793/S294992912500052X.html; also a NotebookLM capture) Table 3 gives a third EAC-1 oxide set citing 'Collins et al., 2022'. The row reads 'EAC-1 ( Collins et al., 2022 ) 42.00 - 14.00 11.00 10.00 13.00 2.30 2.70 1.00 0.70 0.26' under the header 'SiO2 FeO Fe2O3 CaO Al2O3 MgO TiO2 Na2O K2O P2O5 MnO'. The primary paper is P.J. Collins et al., Adv. Space Res. 69(11) 3941–3951, doi 10.1016/j.asr.2022.03.012. It should be obtained before using those numbers.

There are three EAC-1 oxide sets, one per source/batch:
- supplier specification via Schleppi/Nieke;
- Engelschiøn XRF, which matches the supplier set;
- Zemeny 2023 batch and Collins 2022, both lower SiO2 and higher MgO.
The curator should record which one is stored.

Geological source: Manick and Nieke say 'Eifel region'; Engelschiøn says Siebengebirge Volcanic Field, Königswinter. EAC-1 is a single quarried basanite, so there is no blend ratio to report.

Library sweep: grep -rliw 'EAC-1' returned 21 files; 'EAC1' returned 1. The extractor's list omitted two:
- papers/LRS/DIRT project/files/1747/349896322_Bacterial_modification_of_lunar_and_Martian_regolith_for_plant_growth_in_life_support.html (writes 'EAC1'; usage study, magnetic extraction);

- Zanotti et al. 'Planetary Soil Simulant Characterisation: NU-LHT-2M', which lists 'EAC-1 Mixed (Apollo 17)'.
- AperTO/Torino celestial-dust toxicity review.
- Azami et al. 2024 lunar manufacturing review.
- A UCL additive-manufacturing PhD thesis.

Patzwald et al. 2025 (LX Part 1, papers/LRS/1-s2.0-S0094576525001109-main.pdf) mentions EAC-1(A) only descriptively. The page papers/LRS/DIRT project/files/1765 is a ResearchGate stub. Its sidebar mentions an unnamed geotechnical and resonant-column study of 'CAS-1, EAC-1, OPRL2N, LMS-1, LHS-1, OPRH2N, OB-1A', a possible primary source that is not in the library.

results.notes: All oxide, mineral, PSD, and glass-content values check out exactly against the OPR datasheet (DS-S060). Two things a curator should look at: (1) release_date='2010' is unsupported anywhere and conflicts with the company's own stated 2015 founding date (JHU-APL 2022 report, NEW1); (2) lunar_sample_reference='Mare regolith (Apollo)' is supported by ESRIC/ARES/producer sources but directly contradicted by the Slabic 2024 guide's own Table 2, which labels OPRL2N as 'High-Ti Mare' (almost certainly a mix-up with OPRL2NT in that NASA document). Ilmenite is listed only as 'Trace' in the datasheet's mineral table (not quantified), correctly absent from stored minerals. Feedstock blend (10% anorthosite / 90% basaltic cinder, confirmed across datasheet/website/ESRIC/Denevi2020/JHU-APL2022) is feedstock, not mineral composition, so not entered as mineral values; note Roth et al. 2025's own Table 1 reverses this to '90% anorthosite/10% basaltic cinder' for OPRL2N, apparently a typo in that abstract since it contradicts the same company's other publications. results.notes: MAJOR FINDING: 'OPRL2W' does not appear anywhere in the full-text library under that exact string (grep -rliw "OPRL2W" across Sources_text returned zero files; also checked without hyphens/spaces). Its sole DB reference (R178, the Slabic 2024 NASA guide) does not name it at all (verified by full-text search). It is also absent from: Off Planet Research's own current products page (papers/LRS/Offplanet.pdf, a Jan-2026 print of their website, which lists OPRL2N, OPRL2NT, and OPRFLCROSS2 in detail but no 'W' agglutinate SKU); the ESRIC knowledge-base simulant registry (papers/LRS/DIRT project/files/1735/simulants.html); the NASA ARES simulants registry (papers/LRS/DIRT project/files/1646/simulants.html); the JHU-APL 2020 and 2022 assessment reports; and the OPR-authored 2025 LPSC mechanical-properties abstract. The ONLY unambiguous positive evidence that 'OPRL2W' is a real product name is one sentence in Patzwald et al. 2025 (NEW1): agglutinates can be added to the OPR base simulants, producing OPRL2W (=OPRL2N + agglutinates), OPRH2W, OPRH3W, OPRH4W. Off Planet Research's own QA description (2022 Assessment, p.21) states that their agglutinate simulants are 'provided separately and left to the user to mix with a base simulant in desired quantities' and 'share the same chemical compositions' as the base simulant — meaning OPRL2W, as such, may not have one fixed oxide/mineral/geotechnical value set at all; its composition would depend on the user-selected agglutinate mixing ratio. Two review papers (NEW2, and an unopened-for-depth ScienceDirect review 'Research progress on the adaptability of lunar regolith simulant-based composites...', papers/LRS/DIRT project/files/1643/S2095268624001381.html, which cites 'OPRL2N/H2N/H2W/L2W/H3N/H3W' under one reference [18]) only mention 'L2W' inside combined slash-separated product lists, too ambiguous to support any specific stored value — both were opened and considered but not used as support. Recommend the curator decide whether 'OPRL2W' should remain a standalone catalog entry (and if so, correct lunar_sample_reference and release_date, which are unsupported and likely erroneous) or be reclassified/annotated as a user-mixed variant of OPRL2N rather than a fixed-composition product.

values.note: IMPORTANT CONTRADICTION: R037 (the simulant's only formal listed reference, LEAG-CAPTEM 2010) attributes MKS-1 instead to 'Carpenter, 2005, USA-MSFCS' (US Marshall Space Flight Center), and this same USA/MSFC attribution is reproduced verbatim in Taylor et al. 2016 and in the Ruan et al. 2024 (IGG-01) comparison table ('MKS-1 USA 2005'). Alberquilla et al. 2022 (NEW1) and the TJ-1 ResearchGate snippet (NEW3) instead attribute it to 'JAXA' / 'the Japanese space agency'. Three independent, more specific sources (NEW2 Li et al. 2009; NEW4 He 2010 dissertation; NEW5 Ryu et al. 2018 Table 2, which lists 'Shimizu Corporation' as MKS-1's Institution column value) agree on Shimizu Corporation, which is why institution is marked supported here — but the curator should be aware of the conflicting USA-MSFC/JAXA attributions in the other sources, since this may indicate confusion between two different simulants sharing the name 'MKS-1', or simply an error that propagated through the LEAG report and its citers.
